newsitem.title: USA: Rare seashell swiped, hawked on Internet.
newsitem.headline: Rare seashell swiped, hawked on Internet.

text.p: A shell expert hired to appraise a New York museum's collection stole a rare seashell and hawked it on the Internet, a U.S. Customs agent said on Thursday.

The shell, purloined from the American Museum of Natural History last summer, was one of only six known specimens in the world of Chimaeria incomparabilis, a shiny brownish- coloured shell with a broad, striated edge. It brought $20,000 on the seashell black market, assistant special agent Keith Prager said.

Martin Gill, 49, of Miami, was arraigned in a federal courtroom on Wednesday on a charge of interstate transport of stolen goods and faced a possible five-year prison term and $250,000 in fines. He was freed on a $10,000 bond.
Gill, a seashell expert, was hired last summer to appraise the museum's collection, Prager said. The shell was discovered missing shortly after Gill worked there.
"He wandered out with this thing and put it on the Internet for sale," Prager said. "If something has value, someone will steal it."

The shell, about 2 1/2 inches (6.3 cm) long and found only in water 300 feet (90 meters) deep, was snapped up by a Belgian buyer for $12,500. He quickly sold it to an Indonesian collector who paid $20,000 for the shell and still has it. Customs officials are trying to arrange its retrieval.
Prager said his office had handled cases involving the smuggling of drugs, snakes, bugs, plants and freon gas, but this was his first seashell case.
